cells.tense: Right now what you have in your hands is already reaching the people who need it.
cells.act: face one way for three days
cells.ask: For three days, put your weight behind the one you'd choose and nowhere else — no scanning the room, no spread across two. See what one direction does.
cells.core:
You can hand your strength to someone and keep your own feet under you. What arrives for them arrives because you can see what a person actually needs and give that much, not everything. And when a thing is finished, it gets set down — that part comes to you naturally.

The release is the harder half. You'll keep feeding what's already complete because finishing it would mean stepping out of the role that's held you steady. Pick one person to back, go all the way in, and stop surveying for who else might need you. Three days facing one way shows you the release you've been putting off, and what your strength is for when nobody's asking.
cells.sheetLine: You give what's needed and set the rest down.
cells.verb: handing your strength to whoever needs it
cells.place: where you let go of what you have carried past its time

cells.tense: The next need is being covered before anyone has asked, and the covering starts sooner each time.
cells.act: return the small thing you owe before anyone asks
cells.ask: Take the help already offered to you — the hour, the ride, the meal — then go a full day without covering any need you see forming. Lifting early counts too.
cells.core:
What you offer runs past the ask. You see who'll need what before they do, and out the door goes your strength to meet it — so more than one person's weight sits on you before they've requested it. A gift that lands before it's wanted reads as a bill, and people feel managed where they meant to feel helped. You're braced for a shortage that hasn't come.

Let something return to your side first. Take the help that's already been offered, and hold off a day before lifting for anyone else. Rest isn't a reward to earn. When a thing is truly done, the finishing is the release; you don't have to let somebody's unmet need pick the moment you stop.
cells.sheetLine: You carry the need before it's asked for.
cells.verb: handing your strength to whoever needs it
cells.place: where you let go of what you have carried past its time

cells.tense: The strength that once went out to people stayed at a door that has closed.
cells.act: release the method, not the purpose
cells.ask: Drop one way of helping that no longer fits, keep the care that was under it, and change nothing else for now.
cells.core:
The strength is there, and it stopped moving outward. What used to flow toward people now halts at your own edge — not from coldness, but because the way you once did it doesn't fit anymore and the grip hasn't let go. So the handholds stay open, and that stillness reads to you as the end of being needed.

Don't push feeling into this and don't try to care harder. Start from the other end: the purpose stays, the method goes. Name one habit of helping that's stopped fitting — a role, a routine, a way of showing up — set just that down, and keep the care that lived under it. Letting go has to come before the strength returns; pushing measures at a starved place only tightens the grip. Try one approach released, and watch what reopens.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped moving toward people when the old way closed.
cells.verb: handing your strength to whoever needs it
cells.place: where you let go of what you have carried past its time

cells.tense: The support is going out and the one sending it does not count it as their own.
cells.act: decide the heading from what you want, not from logic
cells.ask: Put down two lines where you'll see them: someone you're holding up, and something you want. Leave it there. Then take one small step toward what you want.
cells.core:
You are one of the people keeping somebody else upright, and if asked you'd say you're not doing anything special. The lifting doesn't show up in your own account of the week. That's how release works here — when something gets set down, nothing marks it as a choice you made, so the value stays hidden and the credit stays unclaimed.

Put it where you can see it: a person you're holding up, and something you want for yourself, on the same page. Nobody has to read it. Then take one small step toward what you want — not what the logic says is needed. Seeing your own handwriting is how the giver gets counted in. The strength was not the trouble, and wanting something for yourself isn't either.
cells.sheetLine: You hold people up and don't count it as yours.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that resources are already flowing toward others and that release is the thing standing in the way of it — a reader could reasonably say the giving is not flowing at all, or that what they need to release is not theirs to release. If my read is wrong and they are actually depleted rather than braced, the Too Much ask (using what comes in before lifting the next load) still teaches something, and the Too Little ask (release the method, not the purpose) still holds because it does not require the support to be flowing. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any version of 'you are the strong one' — cut from all four.
